content: A reduction in saturated fatty acid (SFA) intake has been associated with a decreased risk of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) and CVD-related mortality. Most studies included in the analyses reported baseline SFA consumption exceeding 10% of total energy intake. While no clear effects were observed for SFA intake below 10%, significant reductions in CVD risk were noted when SFA intake was reduced to less than 9% of total energy. This evidence supports reducing SFA intake to 10% of total energy, though evidence for further reduction below this threshold is limited. The World Health Organization (WHO) is currently updating its guidance on polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs). Prospective observational studies reviewed by Reynolds et al. suggest that lower SFA intake (less than 10% of total energy) compared to higher intake is associated with reduced all-cause mortality in adults, though the evidence is of low certainty. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled feeding studies reviewed by Mensink demonstrate that replacing SFAs with PUFAs, monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs), or carbohydrates significantly lowers low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels in adults, with high certainty. The reduction in LDL cholesterol is cumulative, meaning greater reductions in SFA intake lead to greater decreases in LDL cholesterol, with effects observed even at SFA intakes as low as 2% of total energy. Importantly, reducing SFA intake does not negatively affect children’s growth, micronutrient status, cognitive development, or sexual development. Evidence from systematic reviews, such as that by Hooper et al. Instead, small benefits or no effects were observed. However, replacing SFAs with carbohydrates of mixed composition slightly increased triglycerides and reduced high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, though the clinical relevance of these changes is unclear. WHO recommends reducing SFA intake to 10% of total energy and replacing SFAs with PUFAs, MUFAs, or carbohydrates from whole grains, vegetables, fruits, and pulses. Evidence suggests that replacing SFAs with PUFAs from plant sources provides the greatest health benefits, including reduced risk of CVDs, coronary heart disease, and all-cause mortality. Replacing SFAs with MUFAs or carbohydrates from whole grains also offers benefits, though the evidence is less robust. Replacement with refined carbohydrates or free sugars is not recommended due to limited or no health benefits. WHO also recommends reducing trans-fatty acid (TFA) intake to less than 1% of total energy. Lower TFA intake is associated with reduced risk of CVDs, coronary heart disease, and all-cause mortality. Replacing TFAs with PUFAs or MUFAs from plant sources significantly lowers LDL cholesterol and improves blood lipid profiles. Replacement with carbohydrates also lowers LDL cholesterol, though PUFAs and MUFAs have greater effects. Industrially produced TFAs, the predominant source of dietary TFAs in many populations, should be largely avoided. WHO’s REPLACE action package provides a roadmap for countries to eliminate industrially produced TFAs from the food supply. The recommendations emphasize the importance of both the quantity and quality of dietary fats. For energy balance, reductions in SFA or TFA intake should be compensated by increased intake of other nutrients, such as PUFAs, MUFAs, or carbohydrates from whole grains, vegetables, fruits, and pulses. In cases where total energy intake needs to be reduced, SFA or TFA intake can be lowered without replacement. These guidelines aim to promote healthy diets, prevent diet-related non-communicable diseases, and improve overall population health.
